newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Controversy over sacking of Belgian sex case judge.
newsitem.headline: Controversy over sacking of Belgian sex case judge.

text.p: Belgian authorities faced public anger, including isolated work-stoppages, on Tuesday over the removal of the popular magistrate leading a child sex and murder investigation.

The decision to take Jean-Marc Connerotte off the case in which four children have so far been found dead and two others rescued alive has undermined already shaky public confidence in the legal system and fueled theories of a high level cover-up.
Belgium's top court ruled on Monday that Connerotte had compromised his impartiality by accepting a free dish of pasta from a group helping parents of missing children.
Workers at a Volkswagen motor plant on the edge of Brussels staging a 24-hour spontaneous strike were gathering outside the high court where the ruling was handed down on Monday.

There were stoppages by some staff at state telephone company Belgacom, and at a factory in the east Belgian town of Liege where the father of one of the eight-year-old victims in the affair worked. In some areas buses stopped running.

A mass public demonstration had already been planned for next Sunday in Brussels, and with the prospect now of public emotion boiling over, parents of the missing and dead children in the affair have pleaded for calm and dignity.
Tens of thousands are expected at the October 20 rally. Belgian railways is offering cut-price tickets to Brussels.

Some diehard protestors spent Monday night outside the court where news of the ruling had been greeted by howls of derision from a crowd of around 700 people. In the port city of Antwerp 300 more had staged a demonstration of support.
Newspapers were split between condemnation of an outdated, inhumane system and deference to the demands made of an invistigative magistrate, who must be seen to be neutral.
"He didn't deserve that!" cried popular daily La Derniere Heure above a picture of a dejected-looking Connerotte.
Francophone paper Le Soir called the decision a "difficult compromise" in a front-page editorial.
"Those in politics who have put pressure in recent days on the high court juges...must tell themselves it is up to them to dust down the judicial code and modernise the law," it said.
Justice minister Stefaan De Clerck pledged the decision would not hinder efforts to solve the case.
Thirteen people, including convicted rapist Dutroux and businessman Michel Nihoul, have been arrested over the affair.
Lawyers for Dutroux and Nihoul had introduced the request for the removal of Connerotte.
"This decision is like spitting on the tombs of Julie and Melissa," Gino Russo, the father of Melissa, said on Monday.
Eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo disappeared in June 1995. Their bodies were found two months ago entombed on a property owned by Dutroux. They had starved to death.
The Russo and Lejeune families have lodged an objection to the ruling, which is unlikely to succeed but could allow Connerotte to remain on the job temporarily.
